# Preliminaries

This is a reproducible report to accompany "The Love of Large Numbers: A Popularity Bias in Consumer Choice," by Derek Powell, Jingqi Yu, Melissa DeWolf, and Keith J. Holyoak. This will allow for the reproduction of the figures and analyses reported in the paper. Some additional analyses not reported in the paper are descrbed in the final section of this document.

Running this notebook requires the files contained in the OSF repository for this article.

This notebook is not completely self-contained. Many data files were prepared outside of R. Components of the processing of Amazon.com reviews were completed in Python, and the model predictions are generated using custom Matlab code. The Matlab model code is also included so that the model predictions can be reproduced, but this cannot be run in this notebook.

## Figure 1.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align = "center", fig.height=4,fig.width=6.5}

##############
## define function for kernel density conditional P plots
##############
make_density_plot_x <- function(data_input,maxN){
  
mydata <- data_input[which(data_input$N < maxN),]


k1 <- kde2d(mydata$score,mydata$N,n=256) # 

# generate distribution of P(x|N)
mymat = k1$z
for(i in 1:dim(mymat)[1])  # for each row
{
  for(j in 1:dim(mymat)[2]) # for each column
  {
    valsum=sum(k1$z[,i]) 
    mymat[j,i] = k1$z[j,i]/valsum # calculate P(x|n) from P(x,n)
  }
}

k1c <- k1
k1c$z <-mymat
output <- k1c

return(output)
}



# make kernel density estimates of P(X|n)

dens.cell <- make_density_plot_x(cell.nm,quantile(cell.nm$N,.95))
dens.elec <- make_density_plot_x(elec.nm,quantile(elec.nm$N,.95))
dens.health <- make_density_plot_x(health.nm,quantile(health.nm$N,.95))
dens.dining <- make_density_plot_x(dining.nm,quantile(health.nm$N,.95))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
##########
## create 2x2 plot of heatmaps for P(x|n) (figure 1)
##########

# Color housekeeping

v <- viridis(32)
legend_title = expression(paste(italic("P"),"(",italic("x"),"|",italic("n"),")"))

heatmap_theme= theme(panel.grid.major=element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
        axis.line=element_line(color='black'),
        text=element_text(family='Arial',size=12),
        plot.title=element_text(family='Arial'))

df.cell <- data.frame(expand.grid(x=dens.cell$x, y=dens.cell$y), z=as.vector(dens.cell$z))
df.elec <- data.frame(expand.grid(x=dens.elec$x, y=dens.elec$y), z=as.vector(dens.elec$z))
df.health <- data.frame(expand.grid(x=dens.health$x, y=dens.health$y), z=as.vector(dens.health$z))
df.dining <- data.frame(expand.grid(x=dens.dining$x, y=dens.dining$y), z=as.vector(dens.dining$z))

plt.cell <- ggplot(df.cell, aes(x,y,colour=z))  + geom_point() + 
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours=v,
                         guide = guide_colourbar(title=legend_title,
                                                 nbin=128, 
                                                 barheight = 4, 
                                                 barwidth = .5)) +
  labs(x="Average Score",
       y="Number of Reviews",
       title="Cell Phones & Accessories") + 
  heatmap_theme

plt.elec <- ggplot(df.elec, aes(x,y,colour=z)) + geom_point() + 
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours=v, guide = guide_colourbar(title=legend_title,nbin=128, barheight = 4, barwidth = .5)) +
  labs(x="Average Score",y="Number of Reviews",title="Electronics") + heatmap_theme

plt.health <- ggplot(df.health, aes(x,y,colour=z)) + geom_point() + 
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours=v, guide = guide_colourbar(title=legend_title,nbin=128, barheight = 4, barwidth = .5)) +
  labs(x="Average Score",y="Number of Reviews",title="Health & Beauty") + heatmap_theme

plt.dining <- ggplot(df.dining, aes(x,y,colour=z)) + geom_point() + 
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours=v, guide = guide_colourbar(title=legend_title, nbin=128, barheight = 4, barwidth = .5)) +
  labs(x="Average Score",y="Number of Reviews",title="Kitchen & Dining") + heatmap_theme


plt.heatmaps <- grid.arrange(plt.cell,plt.elec,plt.health,plt.dining,ncol=2)
ggsave('Outputs/Fig1.png',plot=plt.heatmaps,width=6.5,height=4.5)
ggsave('Outputs/Fig1_print.tiff',plot=plt.heatmaps, device="tiff", dpi=300, width=6.5,height=4.5)
```

# Model Predictions

## Figure 3

```{r, include=FALSE}

# load in human data

exp1exp2 <- read.csv('Data Files/exp1exp2_data_leftRight.csv',header=TRUE)

# code popularity into binary var
exp1exp2$popRatio_bin <- ifelse(exp1exp2$leftN>exp1exp2$rightN,1,0)
exp1exp2$experiment <- ifelse(exp1exp2$experiment==2,1,0)


exp1exp2$sd <-  sqrt(exp1exp2$choseBigP*(1 - exp1exp2$choseBigP) / (exp1exp2$choseLR+exp1exp2$choseMR))

exp1 <- exp1exp2[which(exp1exp2$experiment==0),]
exp2 <- exp1exp2[which(exp1exp2$experiment==1),]
```

# Human Data

## Experiment 1

### Qualitative analyses

For trials where model predicts P(LR superior) >= .55, what proportion of Ps still continue to choose MR product? Compare against chance responding for these trials reveals Ps are biased toward MR product even in cases where model predicts it is worse.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

# recreate qualitative analyses here

# grab relevant trials w/ which
exp1_model_favs_LR <- exp1[which((exp1$reverse==0 & exp1$mod_pred_emp <= .45) | (exp1$reverse==1 & exp1$mod_pred_emp >= .55)) ,]

# count # of relevant trials
nrow(exp1_model_favs_LR)

# sum actual choices and do sign test

binom.test(as.integer(sum(exp1_model_favs_LR$choseMR)), 
           as.integer(sum(exp1_model_favs_LR$choseMR) + sum(exp1_model_favs_LR$choseLR)))
  
```

### Model Comparison

Summary of logistic regression (heuristic cue-weighting) model of Experiment 1.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

AIC_exp1_mod_emp = 2*0 - sum(log(exp1$mod_pred_emp)*exp1$choseL+log(1-exp1$mod_pred_emp)*exp1$choseR)

AIC_exp1_mod_unif = 2*0 - sum(log(exp1$mod_pred_unif)*exp1$choseL+log(1-exp1$mod_pred_unif)*exp1$choseR)

summary(fitexp1)

print(paste('AIC of Bayesian model (emp.) = ',AIC_exp1_mod_emp))
print(paste('AIC of Bayesian model (unif.) = ',AIC_exp1_mod_unif))
print(paste('AIC of Logistic Regression model = ',AIC(fitexp1)))

print(paste('R2 for Bayesian model (emp) = ',cor(exp1$mod_pred_emp,exp1$choseLeftP)^2))
print(paste('R2 for Bayesian model (unif) = ',cor(exp1$mod_pred_unif,exp1$choseLeftP)^2))
print(paste('R2 for logistic regression model = ',cor(predict(fitexp1,type="response"),exp1$choseLeftP)^2))
```

### Model Comparison

```{r, echo=FALSE}
summary(fitexp2)

AIC_exp2_mod_emp = 2*0 - sum(log(exp2$mod_pred_emp)*exp2$choseL+log(1-exp2$mod_pred_emp)*exp2$choseR)

AIC_exp2_mod_unif = 2*0 - sum(log(exp2$mod_pred_unif)*exp2$choseL+log(1-exp2$mod_pred_unif)*exp2$choseR)

print(paste('AIC of Bayesian model (emp.) = ', AIC_exp2_mod_emp))
print(paste('AIC of Bayesian model (unif.) = ', AIC_exp2_mod_unif))

print(paste('R2 for Bayesian model (emp) = ',cor(exp2$mod_pred_emp,exp2$choseLeftP)^2))
print(paste('R2 for Bayesian model (unif) = ',cor(exp2$mod_pred_unif,exp2$choseLeftP)^2))
print(paste('R2 for logistic regression model = ',cor(predict(fitexp2,type="response"),exp2$choseLeftP)^2))
```

## Meta-analysis

Determining whether Ps were sensitive to sample size by comparing results across experiments 1 and 2. Should see an effect (and/or interaction) of experiment in the model. It is non-significant, suggesting that responses didn't differ across experiments and absolute sample sizes.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

summary(fit_red <- glm(cbind(choseR, choseL) ~ revAdvL  + popRatio_bin, data=exp1exp2, family=binomial(logit)))

summary(fit_full <- glm(cbind(choseR, choseL) ~ revAdvL  + popRatio_bin + experiment + experiment*revAdvL, data=exp1exp2, family=binomial(logit)))

anova(fit_red, fit_full,test="Chisq")
```

### Discussion

As can be seen in the figure, the predicted influence of absolute review score (whether both products are poor, middling, outstanding, etc.) is largely a product of the empirical prior. 

Let us consider the effect of the empirical prior on the model’s selection of products as compared with the uniform prior. For a model with uninformative (uniform) priors, the absolute review score affects selections only near the bounds of the scale (1 and 5). However, as seen in the plots on the right, the model with empirical priors generally favors selecting product A (the product with more reviews) when reviews are favorable, and favors selecting product B (the product with fewer reviews) when reviews are poor. This prediction is uniquely driven by the prior expectation that a majority of products are of fairly high quality: when we generally expect products to be of high quality, we should prefer a product with poor reviews that provide us less, rather than more, certainty of its low quality. Finally, as shown in the plot on the left, this effect is somewhat diminished as sample size increases (indicated by a decrease in the slope of the lines). This prediction is in keeping with a general feature of Bayesian models, that the influence of prior expectations diminishes as the amount of available information increases.

## Choices by Expected Utility

We conceived of product selection in this task as an attempt to select the product that was more likely to be of higher quality. Thus, the model computes P($\theta_A$ > $\theta_B$). Another way to perform this task would be to attempt to maximize the expected utility of the product choice. This model would calculate the difference in expected utility between the two products, and then somehow translate those utility calculations into a probability of selecting each product. Crudely, the model would be more likely to select the product with greater utility and this probability would increase as the difference in utilities increased.

A utility function, $U(x)$, is a function that maps inputs (e.g., dollar amounts, or here, star ratings) to subjective value. Our approach in the paper allowed us to remain agnostic regardingto the utility function participants used in assigning values to different star ratings. This is because P($\theta_A$ > $\theta_B$) is unaffected by the choice of utility function so long as the same monotonic utility function is applied to both items. To grasp this intuitively, consider the actual process by which we calculate P($\theta_A$ > $\theta_B$): we sample values from each distribution and compare which is greater many times until a probability can be estimated. Whether we compare the original star ratings or transform them, the inequality will remain the same (again, so long as the transformation is applied identically to both and is monotonic). 
In contrast, maximizing the utility of the selected product requires that some utility function be assumed or estimated. This goes well beyond the scope of our paper. However, we can begin to explore these issues with some additional model simulations. 

In this simulation we examine how a log utility function affects the predictions of the model. One classical model of a utility function is $U(x)$ = $log(x)$. This function is able to capture many important features of human decision-making, such as risk aversion. Risk aversion is the tendency to prefer a certain gain over a risky one--even when the expected value of the two gains are equal. For instance, people generally prefer a certain \$50 gain to a 50% probability of a \$100 gain.

We calculate the expected utility difference under the model assuming a linear utility function (star ratings untransformed; left) and a log utility function over star ratings (right) for small (*n* = 6 v. *n* = 26; top) and large sample sizes (*n* = 25 v. *n* = 150; bottom).

### Discussion

As is clear from the figure, the choice of utility function has a non-trivial impact on the difference in expected utility between the two products. However, qualitatively comparing these predictions to the human behavioral data, it is clear the model favors selecting the LR product in many of the situations where participants overwhelmingly prefer the MR product. That is, it fails as a model of the observed human behavior in this task.

Future research might attempt to empirically elicit people's utility functions over star ratings, and might also explore how these functions differ across domains.
